sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles a segment of the transpressional structures that deform the off-shore foreland in front of the external front of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt (SFTB). The SFTB forms the backbone of mainland Sicily and is part of the Maghrebian-Apennines orogenic belt forming the broad central-western Mediterranean collisional plate boundary. The leading edge of this thrust system crops out on-shore in its eastern portion between Gela and Catania, this section being confined to the east by the structures related to the subduction system of the Ionian basin, and in its western portion between Capo Granitola and Sciacca. In its central section it follows a broad southerly convex arch running for most of its length off-shore the southern Sicilian coast (Gela Nappe). In western Sicily, the general trend of the Plio-Quaternary SFTB external thrust front gradually turns to a NE-SW/NNE-SSW strike forming a northward recess around the Saccense Meso-Cenozoic carbonate platform. This front eventually crosses the Sicily Channel along the Adventure Thrust Front (ATF), thus connecting with the thrust fronts outcropping on-land in Tunisia. Off-shore the southern Sicily coast, to the east of the ATF, two N-S trending transpressional fault systems cut across the foreland faults, forming the Capo Granitola (CGFS) and Sciacca (SFS) fault systems (Ferranti et al., 2019). The latter, also known as the Belice-Sciacca Wrench Fault System (Argnani et al., 1986), is interpreted to separate two sectors of the Sicily Channel rift zone. The Sicilian-Maghrebian fold-and-thrust belt developed since early Miocene times in the framework of the ca. N-S directed Africa-Europe plate convergence and deformed rocks mostly belonging to the northern African paleomargin. This is characterized by carbonate platforms and interposed deep basins (Pelagian domain), involving in the deformation Neogene-Quaternary foredeep deposits along the external fronts. Geological and geophysical subsurface data show that in western Sicily the SFTB is made up of two superposed structural levels: the shallower, thin-skinned one composed of thrust sheets involving deep-water rocks, overthrusted during the Miocene on the deeper one, that in turn deforms the shallow-water platform carbonates of the Trapanese and Saccense units. From the late Miocene (Messinian), the lower level was deformed by deep-seated thrust ramps associated with long wavelength anticlines that passively refolded the upper structural level (Oldow et al., 1990; Avellone et al., 2010; Catalano et al., 2013).
The most recent GPS solutions for the broad Sicily area, due to a denser network of stations, supply a greater detail for the area included between the Hyblean foreland and the Sicilian-Maghrebian chain in eastern Sicily (e.g., Devoti et al., 2017). At the regional scale, GPS data highlight an average Nâ€“S pattern of convergence across the outer fronts of the on-land sectors of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system, in agreement with geological evidence of their recent activity testified by the deformation of Plio-Quaternary foredeep deposits and south of the Mt. Etna volcano, of late Pleistocene-Holocene marine and fluvial deposits.
Historical and instrumental catalogues show that in Sicily and surrounding areas the most important seismic events are located in few distinct sectors, including the Belice area, the Southern Tyrrhenian Sea offshore the northern Sicily coast, the Nebrodi and Peloritani mountain ranges, the Mount Etna and the Hyblean regions, while only scattered and minor seismicity is observed in central Sicily (Caltanissetta Basin) and in the Sicily Channel. In western Sicily, the only destructive earthquakes occurred during the 1968 seismic sequence, with a mainshock on 15 January 1968 (Mw 6.41 from Rovida et al., 2021) that had its mesoseismal area in the Valle del Belice. The sequence, whose core includes at least three major events, spanned from 14 to 25 January (e.g., Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Azzaro et al., 2020), and lasted until September 1968 (De Panfilis and Marcelli, 1968). Different focal solutions have been proposed in the literature for this sequence, including compressional (McKenzie, 1972) or strike-slip mechanisms (Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Gasparini et al., 1980, 1982; Neri et al., 2005). According to the latter group of investigators, the 1968 sequence may have occurred by right-lateral/compressional slip along NNW-SSE striking planes. In both cases, the average P-axis is low-dipping and nearly N-S trending. Accordingly, there are two fault models proposed in the literature: a) N-S right-lateral faulting along a lithospheric transcurrent fault system, which would extend from the Sicily Channel to the southern Sicilian coast, or to the northern Sicilian coast (San Vito Lo Capo - Sciacca shear zone, SVCS; Di Stefano et al., 2015) and would have allowed the differential flexural retreat of the Pelagian foreland, or b) reverse faulting along the E-W striking thrust front.
More to the west, with respect to the Belice area, the 7 June 1981, Mw 4.9, Mazara del Vallo earthquake was characterized by a reverse mechanism with a nearly N-S P-axis (Pondrelli et al, 2006) further testifying the activity of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system.
The NNW-trending solution for the mainshock of the 1968 earthquake sequence is in agreement with the N-S alignment of the epicentres of the largest events, whereas the felt area associated with the mainshock is more compatible with a ca. E-W-trending structure. Based on paleoseismological investigations, Michetti et al. (1995) suggested that the Monte Porcello thrust fault ruptured in the 1968 earthquake and has recorded even larger past events. A correlation between instrumental and geological data was attempted by Monaco et al. (1996). These authors, based on geological and morphostructural analysis, suggested a NNW-dipping crustal blind thrust ramp as the possible seismogenic source for the 1968 Belice earthquake sequence. Accordingly, Lavecchia et al. (2007) considered this area as part of a single regional-scale seismogenic structure (named Sicilian Basal Thrust, SBT), which deepens northward from the front and reaches sub-crustal depths (see also Visini et al., 2010; Sgroi et al., 2012). The evidence put forward by Lavecchia et al. (2007) to classify the Belice sequence as â€œdeep compressionalâ€�, hence discriminating between the two different solutions proposed in the literature, are based on 1) the better fit of the reverse solution with the macroseismic field, 2) the northward deepening of the seismic sequence, 3) the lack of geological evidence for Nâ€“S strike slip faulting in the epicentral area, and 4) the coherence with the mechanism of the nearby 7 June 1981, Mw 4.9, Mazara del Vallo earthquake, showing a thrust solution on E-W trending planes.
To the SW of the Belice area, a NE-SW trending thrust fault array straddles across the coastline and it is composed of several segments showing geodetic and geologic evidence of active deformation (Barreca et al., 2014, 2020; Ferranti et al., 2019, 2021). The northern, on-land segment corresponds with an up to 60 m high morphological scarp, which is the fore-limb of a broad fold involving Lower Pleistocene sediments and cm-scale reverse displacement of an early Bronze-Hellenistic age road. It is marked by a sharp gradient in Differential SAR interferometry and GPS velocity fields. Inversion of fault slip-lineation data from structures displacing the archaeological remains yields a N110Â°E shortening axis, consistent with the geodetic shortening direction estimated from GPS differential velocities. In the off-shore, the southern segments of the SFTB run along the Adventure Thrust Front, while, slightly to the east, the foreland is crossed by the transpressional faults and folds of the CGFS and SFS, which show on Sparker seismic profiles folding of Late Pleistocene-Holocene deposits and out-of-syncline thrust splays cutting the sea-floor. This sector of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system may be tentatively correlated to the seismic events that induced the destruction of Selinunte temples due to their proximity to the archaeological site (Hinzen et al., 2018), however, up to now there is no conclusive evidence on where the causative earthquakes were really generated.
A detailed and systematic critical analysis of the archaeological data in the Selinunte area shows that at least two seismic events had actually struck the Selinunte temples causing their collapse (e.g., Guidoboni et al., 2002; Bottari et al., 2009). These seismic events, dated to a period between the fourth and third centuries B.C. and between the fourth and sixth century A.D., respectively, are currently not included in the Italian seismic catalogues.
A segment of this Source is thought to have caused the 02:01:09 (GMT), 15 January 1968, Mw 6.41 earthquake. This Composite Source is thought to be a WSW-ENE trending thrust splay located in the hinterland of the outermost front of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt. We believe that this sector of the Apennine-Maghrebide thrust system is characterised by infrequent moderate earthquakes generated by blind segments of the thrust system.
The strike of this Composite Source was taken from the general orientation of mapped tectonic structures. The dip was inferred from regional geological considerations concerning the thrust plane. The rake was assumed to represent thrusting based on general geodynamic considerations. The minimum depth was based on the geometry of the thrust system as derived from geological information, while the maximum depth was inferred by geometrical considerations concerning the depth at which active thrusting is rooted. Slip rate was inferred from regional geodynamic data.
